messages.text: Our office espresso machine is leaking. A wants a simpler one and B wants to keep the old one. I don't want a fight over coffee. Can you help us sort it out?

Mostly I just want reliable coffee and a calm kitchen. The leak is the main thing that bothers me; I’m not attached to either machine, and I don’t know why the old one matters to B. I’d rather not be the one chasing everyone or mediating, and I don’t have anything I need kept from A or B. I won’t take sides.

I’d be glad if we could keep good coffee without the leak turning into another repair or cleaning project. A simpler, low-upkeep machine sounds easier to live with a few months from now. I’d miss the familiar espresso routine, though I know the old machine means a lot to B because it was Dad’s. So far, I understand B would like to keep it; I’m not sure what C prefers.

It’s our late father’s machine, and keeping it going means something to me beyond the coffee. But it keeps breaking, and the leak is wearing me down. I want it repaired and kept if that’s practical; I don’t have much spare time, so repairs need to fit into small slots. Fixing it hasn’t been agreed as my job. In a few months, I’d want it working reliably without this becoming a constant chore.
That wording fits. You can share just that concern with A and B. Your concern sits right with me too.

That’s close. I’d say: “I want good coffee without an ongoing repair or cleaning burden, and I’d like to keep a familiar espresso routine if we can.” C’s situation doesn’t change that. Your concern about agreement and not leaving anyone as the default troubleshooter sounds right to me.

The draft mostly fits, but repairs aren’t my job by default. I’d say: “I want to keep the connection to Dad’s machine and have reliable coffee without it becoming a constant chore or requiring me to handle repairs in my limited spare time.” I don’t know whether it can be repaired or who could look at it. Your concern sits right with me.

That wording still fits. Option 3 sounds closest to what I’d prefer; I’d be uneasy about a rota or ongoing repair arrangements becoming another thing to manage. The grinder hasn’t been bothering me, as far as I can tell.

The wording is right. I’m most comfortable with option 1, but I don’t want repairs or booking quietly landing on me. The grinder seems fine. A no-obligation inspection makes sense if someone else can book it; I can’t take that on right now.

I don’t have a strong preference among them, though I’d be wary of adding a regular upkeep chore. The grinder seems fine to me. An inspection sounds reasonable if it’s agreed who books it; I can’t take that on.

Your concern fits, and I’d appreciate you handling the arranging. The inspection-then-decide approach seems reasonable, provided the inspection itself is genuinely free and no repair or cost is committed without our agreement. I’m comfortable with you booking on that basis; I don’t have another option to add, and the grinder seems fine.

Your concern fits, and it’s fine for you to arrange the inspection. I’m okay with inspecting first, but I wouldn’t lock in option 3 based only on “repeated repairs” before we know the likely cost and what the repair involves. Let’s decide after the inspection; no fifth option from me.
Your concern fits, and I’m fine with you booking the inspection. The rule seems reasonable as a proposal, provided any repair cost is approved before anyone commits to it. No fifth option from me.
